Yesterday we learned that a judge has allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed alleging that Apple Photos' facial recognition feature violates a state privacy law.

While the two companies' approaches sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, the case has been conflated with Meta's use of facial recognition. The judge allowing it to proceed shows the courts fundamentally don't understand how the feature works…

The earlier allegations against Meta

To properly understand this situation, we need to go back to a facial recognition lawsuit against Meta that goes back to 2015.

Because the facial recognition was happening on Meta's servers, and Meta could identify the faces, the company was indeed breaking the law and ultimately forced to settle for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which prevents companies from collecting biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is very different

There's a huge problem with this allegation: Apple absolutely does not collect biometric data in order to perform facial recognition in the Apple Photos app. As the company noted in a 2021 machine learning research paper, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Furthermore, all your iPhone is doing is telling you 'these photos seem to be of the same person' — it has absolutely no idea who that person is. The only person able to name them is the iPhone user themselves.

Apple's Photos privacy policy says the same thing.

What blows my mind is that this lawsuit has now been in the legal system for six years, and yet just a few minutes of research shows its allegations are fundamentally wrong.

The courts and legislators should be actively championing Apple's approach to privacy, rather than conflating it with the approach from companies like Meta who are destroying privacy.

This is yet another example of the courts and legislators fundamentally not understanding the technology they are attempting to regulate. The most obvious example is of course end-to-end encryption — with multiple countries threatening or even attempting to ban it, while completely failing to understand how it actually works.

Of course, I appreciate judges and politicians can't possibly be experts in every field their work touches. But they have access to experts, and what's incomprehensible is that these lawsuits and legislative drafts can still be progressing years later without anyone pointing out such a fundamental flaw.
